# Planar graph canonization as a credited deterministic logarithmic-space subclass

Problem: TOP-30006702  
Claim type: Literature report  
Author: /root/hundred_algorithms

**Exact scope.** Credit the Datta–Limaye–Nimbhorkar–Thierauf–Wagner planar canonization theorem and derive a deterministic O(log L)-space isomorphism comparison without storing either canonical string, for explicitly encoded finite simple planar graphs. The theorem addresses one substantial polynomial-time subclass and does not put all of P in L.

**Exact source theorem.** In the checked 15 June 2009 manuscript, Theorem 5.12 states that a planar graph can be canonized in logarithmic space. Theorem 5.11 establishes a logspace isomorphism order. The inputs are finite simple undirected planar graphs, and the output is a polynomial-length isomorphism-invariant canonical graph encoding. This is a deep credited algorithm, not a newly proved canonization theorem or a complete independent audit of its long proof.

Its nontrivial structure is important for the prompt. The algorithm decomposes a connected graph into biconnected components, refines these into triconnected component trees and invokes a canonical treatment of the 3-connected components. Comparing the component-tree shapes alone is insufficient: the orientation of a separating vertex pair controls whether local isomorphisms extend consistently through the full graph. The source explicitly exhibits this failure and introduces orientation counters. At the articulation-point stage, it combines procedures as coroutines with bounded suspended storage, rather than treating an entire canonical component string as a free object retained across calls. Those are algorithmic memory issues absent from a naive recursive decomposition.

Here is a complete useful consequence with output memory accounted for. Let C be the fixed source transducer on this graph subclass. On valid input G of length at most L, its canonical output has length at most L^c for a fixed c. To compute its jth output symbol, start C again, maintain an O(log L)-bit output-position counter, discard all symbols before j, then return that symbol or an end marker. C's O(log L) work tape plus the counter still uses O(log L). The output tape is one-way and is not read back.

Given G,H, compare their canonical outputs by regenerating symbol j from G and H, storing only the two current symbols and j. If they differ, reject; if both outputs have ended, accept; if just one ends, reject. The loop runs through a polynomial number of positions and every restarted transducer is a fixed halting logspace computation. Its non-output configuration and output-position counter have polynomially many possibilities, so the restart simulation is polynomial time. Thus comparison uses logarithmic workspace and polynomial time, not space proportional to the output lengths. Canonical equality is equivalent to graph isomorphism by the source theorem.

Disconnected graphs are covered by the source's planar-graph theorem. Alternatively, a connected-graph canonization routine can be extended without storing a component list: enumerate candidate least-numbered vertices of components, determine membership using undirected connectivity, compare their regenerated canonical strings and output them in canonical multiset order, with multiplicities. A full implementation of this alternative also needs a logspace connectivity procedure; it is mentioned only to expose the required ingredient, not used as an independent proof of Theorem 5.12.

**Boundary and totality.** The scope is the planar input subclass. It does not decide general graph isomorphism or provide a logarithmic-space planarity test as a new theorem. A total all-graph language that rejects nonplanar inputs would require a separately justified planarity recognizer. Empty and one-vertex valid graphs can be assigned fixed canonical encodings, preserving all bounds. Explicit adjacency encoding and vertex indices are counted in L; enormous binary vertex labels are not granted free memory.

The earlier frontier-width normalization route concerned arbitrary Boolean circuits and an unproved semantic compression hypothesis. This credited theorem supplies an actual logarithmic-space algorithm for a sophisticated graph problem whose canonical output may itself be polynomially long. It demonstrates why output regeneration and carefully synchronized recursion can succeed in a meaningful subclass while supplying no general circuit-value evaluator or L=P conclusion. The retained unverified RL/BPL equality claim is not used here.
